counting_note: 313 leaf questions in section 1 (lines 16-563); the 1.6.5 antecedent/reflexive table is counted by printed row (56), and 1.7 and 1.9 ('repeat the questions') as one each. Each listed item is charged to one primary question; NA = questions purely about form, order, movement, case or affixes; COVERED = the rest. Section 1.1.2 (subordination) is not present in the file and was not audited.

items.what: A classless root used as predicate can mean 'is an X' or 'undergoes X-ing', and the spec gives no rule for which.
items.example: 'x is a test' vs 'x is being tested'; 'E is a cause' vs 'E is caused'
items.how_now: GIVEN test THEME x .  (both readings; the spec itself uses fail THEME test as an event and (exception KIND NOT handled) THEME E as class membership)
items.suggestion: Rule: every root carries one base type in the lexicon (thing / property / event). A thing root as predicate means 'THEME is one'; an event root means 'it happens to THEME'. The other sense is built, never implied: the event as a block { test THEME x }, the doer as person KIND { test AGENT SELF }. One root never carries both senses.

items.source: 1.5.1.1 anaphora by deletion; 1.2.1.2.1-2 verbs without subject/object
items.what: It is not stated whether a left-out role means 'unspecified' or 'the one we were just talking about'.
items.example: 'The test fails. Ana fixed (it).'
items.how_now: 1: GIVEN fail THEME test . 2: GIVEN PAST fix AGENT name«Ana» .  (fixed it, or fixed something?)
items.suggestion: Rule: an omitted role is unspecified, never anaphoric; refer back with THAT, a handle or STEP. Two stated defaults only: the missing AGENT of a REQUEST is the addressee, the missing AGENT of a PLAN is ME.

items.source: 1.2.1.1.3 copular sentence with adverbial complement; 1.9 likeness
items.category: predication of place, time or a role phrase
items.what: There is no 'is', so there is no settled way to predicate a location, a time, or a role phrase (for, from, about, like) of something.
items.example: 'The file is in the folder.' 'This gift is for Ana.' 'x is like y.'
items.how_now: GIVEN (inside REL folder) THEME file .  or  GIVEN exist THEME file AT inside REL folder .  or a root (locate, belong); for 'is for Ana' no form at all without inventing a root
items.suggestion: Reuse the existing particle BE (already in DEFINE) as an empty predicate that only carries role phrases: GIVEN BE THEME file AT inside REL folder . GIVEN BE THEME gift FOR name«Ana» . GIVEN BE THEME x THAN y .

items.source: 1.1.1.2.4.2.1.2 yes/no in reply to negative and leading questions
items.what: After a negated question, YES and NO can each be read as confirming the negation or as asserting the positive.
items.example: 'Didn't you send it?' - 'No.'
items.how_now: BY A 1: ASK NOT DONE send AGENT YOU THEME release . BY B 2: GIVEN ANSWER 1 NO .  (sent or not sent?)
items.suggestion: Rule: YES / NO always judge the question body exactly as written, including its NOT (YES to 'NOT sent' = it was not sent). ASK YES / ASK NO expectations do not change this.

items.what: WHAT in the quantifier slot is glossed 'how many / which', two different questions in one form.
items.example: 'Which tests failed?' vs 'How many tests failed?'
items.how_now: ASK PAST fail THEME WHAT test .  (either)
items.suggestion: Rule: WHAT before a head = which; WHAT MANY = how many (WHAT in degree position before the quantifier MANY). Keep test KIND WHAT for 'what kind of'.

items.what: OR 'directly under ASK' makes a which-one question, so a yes/no question about a disjunction has no form, and it is unclear whether an OR between two role fillers counts as 'directly under'.
items.example: 'Is either A or B failing?' (yes) vs 'Is A failing, or B?' (A)
items.how_now: ASK fail THEME (A OR B) .  (reading not fixed)
items.suggestion: Rule: only an OR that joins whole clauses of the ASK body, or follows the focus particle FOCUS, asks 'which one'; any other OR under ASK is an ordinary disjunction answered YES / NO. ASK fail THEME FOCUS (A OR B) = which of them.

items.what: The spec never says whether OR allows both to hold.
items.example: 'The bug is in the parser or in the lexer (or both / but not both).'
items.how_now: CLAIM exist THEME bug AT (parser OR lexer) .
items.suggestion: Rule: OR is inclusive everywhere outside ASK. Exclusive choice is written with a count over the options: EXACT 1 OF (parser AND lexer).

items.what: BUT is in the grammar but never defined, and it overlaps with the CONTRAST and CONCEDE relations and the DESPITE role.
items.example: 'It is slow but correct.' 'Although it is slow, it is correct.'
items.how_now: CLAIM slow THEME X BUT correct THEME X .  or two sentences with CONTRAST / CONCEDE  or  correct THEME X DESPITE { slow THEME X }
items.suggestion: Rule: BUT = plain contrast inside one sentence (same meaning as CONTRAST between sentences); 'although' is always DESPITE inside a sentence and CONCEDE between sentences. BUT never means concession.

items.source: 1.8.2-1.8.4 what is omitted in the comparative clause
items.category: what the standard is compared with
items.what: A bare THAN phrase does not say which participant it is being compared with.
items.example: 'Ana trusts the test more than Ben' (than Ben does / than she trusts Ben); 'bigger than before'
items.how_now: CLAIM MORE trust AGENT name«Ana» THEME test THAN name«Ben» .
items.suggestion: Let THAN be followed by a role particle naming the slot the standard fills: THAN AGENT name«Ben» / THAN THEME name«Ben» / THAN WHEN before. Bare THAN x is allowed only when the clause has one other role phrase, and compares with that one.

items.what: No stated way to say that one quantity rises or falls with another.
items.example: 'The hotter the gas, the higher the pressure.'
items.how_now: RECALLED IF { MORE hot THEME gas } { MORE high THEME pressure } .  (plausible, not licensed; or with roots such as rise / depend)
items.suggestion: Rule: IF with MORE or LESS and no THAN in both blocks is the correlative reading; add one example. A factor before the degree states the rate (IF { 2 MORE ... } { 4 MORE ... }).

items.source: 1.8.1 comparison; 1.2.5.2.6 quantifiers; 1.2.5.2.9 comparative structures in the noun phrase
items.what: Degree particles may only stand before a predicate or a modifier, so amounts cannot be compared or graded directly.
items.example: 'more tests than last week', 'too many errors', 'enough data', 'almost all users', 'as many as B'
items.how_now: GIVEN MORE big THEME count OF test THAN count OF (test KIND { PAST run THEME SELF WHEN week KIND last }) .
items.suggestion: Allow a degree particle in the quantifier slot or before a quantifier: MORE test, TOO MANY error, ENOUGH data, ALMOST ALL user, EQUAL MANY; the standard goes in the clause's THAN phrase, the purpose in FOR.

items.category: set over which a superlative ranges
items.what: MOST and LEAST have no slot for the group being compared.
items.example: 'the largest of the three files', 'the fastest method known'
items.how_now: GIVEN MOST big THEME F .  plus an improvised OF, AT or EXCEPT phrase for the set
items.suggestion: Rule: with MOST / LEAST the THAN phrase names the comparison set (MOST big THEME F THAN 3 file), parallel to MORE. Also state EQUAL fast THAN { CAN } as the form for 'as fast as possible'.

items.source: 1.2.3.2 modifiers of adverbials; 1.2.1.3.1.1 adverbs; 1.8 comparison of manner
items.what: A manner word filling a role cannot take a degree or a standard under the grammar as written, because the degree slot exists only on predicates and modifiers.
items.example: 'runs very fast', 'converges faster than B', 'fast enough to finish'
items.how_now: run AGENT A WITH (VERY fast)  (not derivable: a head in ( ) is a phrase and has no degree slot)  or  MORE fast THEME { run AGENT A } THAN { run AGENT B }
items.suggestion: Extend head with the form already allowed for modifiers: "(" {degree} root {role phrase} ")". Then: run AGENT A WITH (MORE fast THAN B).

items.what: No example shows how to attach a distance or interval to a relational root, and a clause-level SPAN would be read as the duration of the event.
items.example: 'two days before the release', '3 km south of the city', 'just after', 'exactly at noon'
items.how_now: WHEN before REL release SPAN 2 day  (reads as 'for two days')  or  WHEN (before REL release SPAN 2 day)  (legal under the 'role phrases inside ( )' clarification, never shown)
items.suggestion: Rule plus example: the measure of a relational root is a SPAN phrase inside its parentheses, WHEN (before REL release SPAN 2 day). Degrees ALMOST, AROUND, EXACT, BARELY may precede a relational root in the same parentheses.

items.what: Aspect gives only vague frequency (OFTEN, RARE), with no slot for a counted number of occurrences or a rate.
items.example: 'We ran the test five times.' 'Sample twice a day.' 'one in ten runs'
items.how_now: GIVEN PAST run AGENT US THEME test SPAN 5 occasion .  (SPAN stretched; easily read as a duration)  or  «5x»
items.suggestion: Add one role particle TIMES taking a number, with an optional unit for the rate: PAST run THEME test TIMES 5 . REQUEST sample TIMES 2 SPAN day .

items.what: For property, measure and dependency nouns the choice between OF (owner or whole) and REL (landmark of a relational root) is not decided.
items.example: 'the cause of the error', 'the length of the file', 'the value of x', 'the author of the paper'
items.how_now: cause OF error  or  cause REL error  (the spec has count OF prime but friend REL name«Ana»)
items.suggestion: Rule with a test: REL when the head is identified by its position or relation to the other thing (place, time, kin, cause, author, result); OF when the head is a part, possession, property or measure of it (length, count, price, value). Mark each relational root in the lexicon.

items.what: No stated form for a number or share taken out of a definite set.
items.example: 'three of the tests', '30% of users', 'half of the samples', 'one of the reasons'
items.how_now: 3 OF THAT test  or  3 THAT test  or  30 «%» user  or  half OF sample
items.suggestion: Rule: a part of a set is always quantity-as-head plus OF: 3 OF (THAT test), 30 «%» OF user, half OF sample. A number directly before a head only counts.

items.source: 1.2.5.2.10 other noun modifiers; 1.3.1.1.4 other coordination types
items.category: open list of examples inside a phrase
items.what: NOTE with a phrase means 'namely' (the full list), and EXAMPLE works only between sentences, so 'such as / e.g. / including' has no short form.
items.example: 'substances such as glucose and starch', 'errors, e.g. timeouts'
items.how_now: substance NOTE { include AGENT SELF THEME (glucose AND starch) }
items.suggestion: Let EXAMPLE also serve as a linker: substance EXAMPLE (glucose AND starch) = some members, list not complete.

items.what: Every coordinated clause must repeat its predicate and pre-predicate particles, and paired lists ('respectively') need full clauses.
items.example: 'A scored 3 and B 5.' 'Runs 1 and 2 took 4 s and 9 s respectively.'
items.how_now: GIVEN PAST score AGENT A THEME 3 AND PAST score AGENT B THEME 5 .
items.suggestion: Rule: after AND / OR / BUT, a conjunct that starts with a role particle reuses the predicate and all pre-predicate particles of the clause before it: PAST score AGENT A THEME 3 AND AGENT B THEME 5 . (Unambiguous: a role particle cannot start a unit.)

items.what: NOT before one phrase does not say whether the event is still claimed to have happened with some other filler.
items.example: 'Not Ana changed the setting' = someone else did / it is false that Ana did
items.how_now: GIVEN PAST change AGENT NOT name«Ana» THEME S .
items.suggestion: Rule: NOT on a phrase denies the clause for that filler and asserts nothing about others; to assert that another did it, add the filler (AGENT OTHER person) or use INSTEAD.

items.category: SELF and MUTUAL outside the simple case
items.what: SELF is defined for a main-clause role (= AGENT) and for a modifying clause (= head); its value in a complement block, in a clause with no AGENT, and as an owner inside a phrase is not given, and MUTUAL has the same holes.
items.example: 'A says B hurt himself.' 'x equals itself.' 'A lost her own file.' 'They read each other's code.'
items.how_now: say AGENT A THEME { PAST hurt AGENT B THEME SELF }  (B or A?);  EQUAL THEME x THAN SELF  (no AGENT);  lose AGENT A THEME file OF SELF
items.suggestion: Rule: SELF = the AGENT of the clause it stands in, or its THEME if there is no AGENT, at any depth and also inside a modifier of a role phrase; only directly in a KIND / NOTE clause does it mean the head. Anything longer-range uses a handle. MUTUAL follows the same rule.

items.category: asking to confirm or repeat what was said
items.what: A question about what the other party said or meant, as opposed to whether it is true, needs a full speech-report frame.
items.example: 'To the harbour?' 'You changed what?' 'Do you mean the login test?'
items.how_now: BY B 2: ASK PAST say AGENT YOU THEME { go AGENT YOU TO harbour } .
items.suggestion: Rule, no new particle: ASK RESTATE n = 'is this what sentence n says?', and its body may be a fragment: BY B 2: ASK RESTATE 1 TO harbour . / ASK RESTATE 1 THEME WHAT .

items.source: 1.1.1.2.4.2 incomplete sentences as answers; 1.15.1 minor sentence types
items.what: Fragments are licensed only after SOCIAL, HEAD or as an answer, so short follow-up questions and list entries have no licensed form.
items.example: 'Why?' 'And Ana?' 'Since when?'; list entries such as 'Input: a file'
items.how_now: ASK CAUSE WHAT .  (not licensed; the full clause must be repeated)
items.suggestion: Rule: a fragment body is allowed under any opener when the sentence carries a relation to a target; it reuses the target's predicate and other roles. ASK DETAIL 3 CAUSE WHAT . GIVEN ADD 3 AGENT name«Ana» .

items.what: Whether a modal may follow REQUEST, and what it then means, is not stated, so mandatory, recommended and optional steps cannot be reliably told apart.
items.example: 'You must back up first.' 'Consider adding a test.' 'You may skip this step.'
items.how_now: REQUEST MUST save ...  or  CLAIM SHOULD add AGENT YOU ...  or  RULE MAY skip ...
items.suggestion: Rule: a modal after REQUEST grades it: REQUEST MUST = mandatory, REQUEST SHOULD = recommended, REQUEST MAY = optional or permitted, bare = plain request; REQUEST NOT = do not, REQUEST MAY NOT ... = need not.

items.what: A proposal for joint action and an instruction aimed at a third party have no decided form.
items.example: 'Let's rerun it.' 'Have the reviewer sign off.'
items.how_now: REQUEST run AGENT (ME AND YOU) AGAIN THEME test .  or  PLAN ... AGENT US .  or  ASK SHOULD ...
items.suggestion: Rule: REQUEST with AGENT (ME AND YOU) is a proposal; REQUEST with a third-party AGENT asks that this agent act; CALL names who is being told, when different from the AGENT.

items.source: 1.1.1.5 sentence types used in other functions
items.category: question not addressed to the reader
items.what: A question the writer puts to itself or raises for exposition is not distinguished from one that expects a reply.
items.example: 'Why does the cache miss here?' (I will work it out) vs the same asked of the user
items.how_now: ASK miss AGENT cache CAUSE WHAT .  (both)
items.suggestion: Rule, existing particles: ASK CALL ME = a question the writer sets itself (no reply expected); a bare ASK is addressed to the reader. Rhetorical questions are written as ASK NO CERTAIN / ASK YES CERTAIN.

items.what: Two unranked ways to say that something comes to be in a state or class.
items.example: 'The solution turns red.' 'She became a judge.'
items.how_now: GIVEN BEGIN red THEME solution .  or  GIVEN become THEME solution TO red .
items.suggestion: Rule: change of state is always BEGIN + predicate (and STOP for leaving it); no root 'become'.

items.source: 1.11.2.2.1.3 emphasis on the verb and its categories
items.category: contrast on time, modal or frequency
items.what: The focus slot stands only before a phrase or the predicate, so contrast on a particle cannot be marked.
items.example: 'It CAN fail (I do not say it will).' 'It WAS stable (not any more).'
items.how_now: cannot in one clause; two sentences: CLAIM CAN fail THEME X . CLAIM CONTRAST NOT FUTURE fail THEME X .
items.suggestion: Rule: FOCUS written directly before a time, aspect, modal or strength particle marks that particle as the contrasted item (PAST change = neutral; FOCUS PAST change = it did then, as opposed to now).

items.what: Naming the rejected alternative beside the right one needs a second clause or an odd coordination.
items.example: 'Ana, not Ben, changed it.' 'Use the staging key instead of the live one.'
items.how_now: PAST change AGENT name«Ana» THEME S BUT NOT PAST change AGENT name«Ben» THEME S .  or  AGENT (FOCUS name«Ana» AND NOT name«Ben»)
items.suggestion: Allow BUT NOT between two units of a phrase: AGENT name«Ana» BUT NOT name«Ben»; THEME key KIND staging BUT NOT key KIND live.

items.what: REBUT is limited to what the addressee is presumed to think; there is no relation for withdrawing or replacing an earlier sentence, the writer's own included.
items.example: 'Correction: step 4 is wrong, the cause is the cache.'
items.how_now: 8: DERIVED 6 7 CONTRAST 4 NOT true THEME STEP 4 .  then a new claim
items.suggestion: Widen REBUT: with a target label it denies that sentence whoever wrote it, and a writer's REBUT of its own sentence withdraws it and puts this one in its place. With no label it keeps today's meaning.

items.what: Attitudes cannot be negated and the list has no 'as expected', 'hopefully' or 'worryingly'.
items.example: 'As expected, the control shows no change.' 'Hopefully this fixes it.'
items.how_now: GIVEN NOT change THEME control THAN { PAST expect AGENT ME } .  /  CLAIM hope AGENT ME THEME { ... } .
items.suggestion: Allow NOT before an attitude (NOT SURPRISE = as expected) and add HOPE and WORRY to the attitude list.

items.source: 1.1.1.2.2.1.1 which constituents of the main clause can be questioned
items.what: WHAT can replace a head, a quantifier or a degree, but frequency, obligation and time-frame live in particles and can only be questioned through a root paraphrase.
items.example: 'How often does it fail?' 'Is this required or just advised?' 'What did she do?'
items.how_now: ASK WHAT frequent THEME { fail THEME X } .  /  ASK (WHAT) AGENT A  or  ASK do AGENT A THEME WHAT  (neither stated)
items.suggestion: Rules: WHAT OFTEN in the aspect slot = how often (with TIMES WHAT for a count); an OR between two particles in ( ) under ASK asks which: ASK (MUST OR SHOULD) save ... ; 'do what' is always do THEME WHAT.

items.category: referring back to a kind or an action
items.what: Handles name individuals; there is no short way to refer back to a kind or to a predicate.
items.example: 'a large file and a small one', 'Ben did so too'
items.how_now: file KIND big AND file KIND small ;  PAST fix AGENT name«Ben» ALSO ... (predicate and roles repeated)
items.suggestion: Leave out as a particle: repetition is cheap for a machine writer, and the shared-predicate rule proposed under 1.3.2.1 covers 'did so too' (... AND AGENT ALSO name«Ben»).

items.what: WHAT is a question word only under the nearest ASK; its status with no ASK above it is not stated.
items.example: 'whatever he said', 'I know what he took'
items.how_now: know AGENT ME THEME { PAST take AGENT A THEME WHAT }  (headerless block, no ASK: undefined)
items.suggestion: Rule: WHAT with no enclosing ASK is an error; 'whatever' is ANY thing KIND { ... SELF }, 'what he took' is thing KIND { ... } or a block with its own ASK.

items.source: 1.12.1.1 / 1.12.2 topic particle and what can be topic
items.category: topic that is not a participant
items.what: TOPIC marks a phrase that already has a role; a topic outside the clause's participants has no stated place.
items.example: 'As for the tests, we need more machines.'
items.how_now: CLAIM need AGENT US THEME MORE machine ABOUT test .  or  ABOUT TOPIC test
items.suggestion: Rule: a topic that is not a participant is ABOUT TOPIC x; plain ABOUT x stays 'in respect of x'.

items.source: 1.3.1.3 coordinating major categories; 1.3.2.2 what cannot be omitted
items.category: time and negation across coordinated clauses
items.what: By the grammar each coordinated clause has its own pre-predicate particles, so a second clause without PAST is timeless, which writers will not expect.
items.example: 'She opened the file and read it.'
items.how_now: STORY PAST open AGENT A THEME file AND read AGENT A THEME file .  (second clause past or timeless?)
items.suggestion: State the rule and show the grouped form: particles hold for one clause only; to share them write PAST ( open ... AND read ... ), as already allowed for NOT ( A AND B ).
